title: Write an Email
lines: In Write an Email you read a short practical situation and write an email that does three specific things. The reader might be a professor, a landlord, a manager, a club leader, a company or a library. You have 7 minutes. The task tests whether you can write clear, polite, well-organized English for a real purpose.
## What is on the screen
- A situation of about 60-100 words: who you are, what has happened and who you are writing to.
- Three bullet points: the three things your email must do, for example explain a problem, ask for something, and suggest a solution.
- A text box for your answer. The reader and subject are given, so you write the body of the email: greeting, paragraphs and sign-off.
- A timer showing your 7 minutes. There is no spell checker.
## Scoring

Each email is scored from 0 to 5. A high score needs all three bullets answered clearly and with details, a tone that suits the reader, good organization, and a range of accurate grammar and vocabulary. Missing a bullet is the fastest way to lose points. Aim for about 100-150 words: long enough to develop each point, short enough to check.
## Method in 7 minutes
- Minute 0-1: Read the situation and the three bullets. Decide who the reader is (formal or friendly) and write two or three key words for each bullet.
- Minute 1-6: Write the email using the template below. Give each bullet its own short paragraph with one or two specific details.
- Minute 6-7: Check. Is every bullet answered? Are names, dates and numbers consistent? Fix verb tenses, articles, plural -s and spelling.
## Reusable template
> Greeting: Dear Professor Novak, / Dear Ms. Patel, / Hi Lucas,
> Opening (1-2 sentences): who you are if needed, and why you are writing. "I'm a second-year student in your Monday seminar, and I'm writing about ..."
> Bullet 1 (2-3 sentences): explain or describe, with a concrete detail (a date, a place, a reason).
> Bullet 2 (2-3 sentences): ask or request politely. "Would it be possible to ...?" "I was wondering whether ..."
> Bullet 3 (2-3 sentences): suggest, offer or give details. "One option might be ..." "I'd be happy to ..."
> Closing (1 sentence): thank the reader and say what happens next. "Thank you for considering this. I look forward to hearing from you."
> Sign-off: Best regards, / Kind regards, / Thanks, + your name
## Tone
- Formal reader (professor, manager, company, landlord): full sentences, polite requests with would and could, no slang. Contractions such as I'm and I'd are fine.
- Friendly reader (classmate, friend, club member): warmer, with phrases like "Hope you're doing well" and "Let me know what you think".
- Complaints: firm but polite. Describe the facts, then the request. Avoid blaming language ("You never fix anything").
## Worked example 1

> Situation: You live in an apartment near the university. For two weeks the heating in your bedroom has not worked properly, and the nights are getting colder. Write to your landlord, Mr. Okafor. In your email: describe the problem; explain how it is affecting you; suggest a time when a repair person could come.
> Dear Mr. Okafor,
> I'm writing about the heating in my apartment, number 4B. For about two weeks, the radiator in my bedroom has only been warm for an hour or so in the morning, and it is completely cold at night.

> This is becoming a real problem now that the temperature is dropping. I have been sleeping in the living room, and it has been hard to study in my room in the evenings, which is where I keep my desk and books.
> Could someone come to look at it this week? I'm at home every weekday after 3 p.m., and I'm also free all day on Saturday. If it is easier, I can leave a key with the building manager.
> Thank you for your help. I look forward to hearing from you.
> Best regards,
> Mateo Silva

Why this works: each bullet has its own paragraph; there are concrete details (number 4B, two weeks, after 3 p.m.); the tone is polite and firm; the request uses "Could someone ...". It is about 140 words.
## Worked example 2 (friendly tone)

> Situation: You are in a hiking club. The club leader, Yuki, has asked members for ideas for next month's trip. Write to Yuki. In your email: suggest a place; explain why it would be good for the group; mention one thing members should prepare.
> Hi Yuki,
> Thanks for asking for ideas! I'd like to suggest the lake trail near Pine Ridge, about an hour from campus by bus.

> I think it would work well for our group because the path is mostly flat, so newer members won't find it too hard, but there's an optional climb to a viewpoint for people who want more of a challenge. There's also a picnic area by the water where we could have lunch together.
> The only thing is that parts of the trail get muddy after rain, so everyone should bring waterproof shoes and a change of socks.
> Let me know what you think. I'm happy to look up the bus times if we decide to go.
> Cheers,
> Aisha
## Common traps
- Answering only two bullets, or answering one bullet with half a sentence.
- Writing general sentences with no detail ("There is a problem and I need help").
- The wrong tone: too casual to a professor, or very stiff to a friend.
- Spending too long on the first paragraph and rushing the third bullet.
- Not leaving one minute to check for small errors.
! Useful polite requests: Would it be possible to ...? Could you please ...? I was wondering if ... I would really appreciate it if ... These score better than "I want you to ...".
## How to practise between mocks
- Write one email a day in 7 minutes using the template, then reread it and underline where each bullet is answered.
- Build a phrase bank for opening, requesting, apologizing, complaining, suggesting and closing.
- Practise both tones: write the same situation once to a professor and once to a friend.
- Check your writing for your personal error list (articles, verb tenses, plural -s) and review it before each mock.
